hypotheses.title: StakingBase.initialize() callable by anyone, no access control
hypotheses.description: `StakingNativeToken.initialize()` is `external` with no access control and simply forwards to `_initialize()`. The only guard is `serviceRegistry != address(0)`, which is only set after a successful initialization. Any untrusted caller can front-run the intended deployment/initialization transaction and set all staking parameters (rewardsPerSecond, maxNumServices, serviceRegistry, activityChecker, proxyHash, etc.) to attacker-chosen values.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Deployer deploys `StakingNativeToken`. 2) Attacker observes the pending `initialize()` tx in the mempool. 3) Attacker submits their own `initialize()` with attacker-controlled `StakingParams` (e.g., huge `rewardsPerSecond`, attacker-controlled `activityChecker` that always returns ratioPass=true, attacker-controlled `serviceRegistry`). 4) Attacker's tx is mined first; the legitimate initialization reverts with `AlreadyInitialized()`. 5) Attacker stakes a service, drains all deposited rewards via a fake activity checker, and controls the staking contract's configuration.
hypotheses.impact: Complete takeover of the staking contract configuration; theft of all deposited staking rewards; the legitimate deployment is bricked (cannot re-initialize).
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an `initializer` modifier or restrict `initialize()` to the deployer/owner, and/or use an atomic constructor-based initialization pattern.

hypotheses.title: ServiceRegistryProxyGeneric.changeOwner() has no access control
hypotheses.description: `ServiceRegistryProxyGeneric.changeOwner()` is `external` with no modifier and forwards directly to `iServiceRegistryF.changeOwner(newOwner)`. Because the proxy itself is the owner of the underlying `ServiceRegistryF` (it deployed it in the constructor), any external caller can invoke the proxy's `changeOwner()` and thereby transfer ownership of the underlying service registry to an arbitrary address.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `ServiceRegistryProxyGeneric.changeOwner(attacker)`. 2) The proxy calls `iServiceRegistryF.changeOwner(attacker)`, and since `msg.sender == owner` (the proxy), the underlying registry's owner is set to the attacker. 3) Attacker now owns the service registry and can call `changeManager`, `changeDrainer`, `changeMultisigPermission`, `setBaseURI`, etc.
hypotheses.impact: Full takeover of the service registry: attacker can set themselves as manager/drainer, drain slashed funds, whitelist malicious multisig implementations, and control all service lifecycle operations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an `owner`-only check in the proxy (or remove the proxy's forwarding functions and require the proxy to be the sole caller via a stored owner).

hypotheses.title: ServiceRegistryProxyGeneric.changeManager() and changeDrainer() unguarded
hypotheses.description: Like `changeOwner()`, `changeManager()` and `changeDrainer()` on `ServiceRegistryProxyGeneric` are `external` with no access control and forward to the underlying registry. Since the proxy is the owner of the underlying registry, any external caller can set the manager and drainer to arbitrary addresses.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `ServiceRegistryProxyGeneric.changeManager(attacker)`. 2) Proxy forwards to `iServiceRegistryF.changeManager(attacker)`, which succeeds because `msg.sender` (the proxy) is the owner. 3) Attacker is now the manager and can call `create`, `update`, `activateRegistration`, `registerAgents`, `deploy`, `terminate`, `unbond` on behalf of any service owner. 4) Attacker also calls `changeDrainer(attacker)` and then `drain()` to steal all slashed funds.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker gains manager privileges (can manipulate any service) and drainer privileges (can steal all slashed ETH held by the registry).
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an `owner`-only check on the proxy for all privileged forwarding functions.

hypotheses.title: ServiceRegistryProxy.changeOwner() unguarded, forwards to owned registry
hypotheses.description: `ServiceRegistryProxy` (the non-generic variant) has the same flaw: `changeOwner()`, `changeManager()`, and `changeDrainer()` are `external` with no access control and forward to `iServiceRegistryF`, which the proxy owns. Any external caller can transfer ownership/manager/drainer of the underlying `ServiceRegistryF` to themselves.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `ServiceRegistryProxy.changeOwner(attacker)`. 2) Proxy calls `iServiceRegistryF.changeOwner(attacker)`; since the proxy is the owner, the call succeeds. 3) Attacker now owns the service registry and can drain slashed funds, whitelist malicious multisigs, and change the manager.
hypotheses.impact: Full takeover of the service registry: theft of slashed funds, arbitrary service manipulation, malicious multisig whitelisting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an `owner`-only check on the proxy for all privileged forwarding functions.

hypotheses.title: GuardCM.checkTransaction() callable by anyone to bypass guard
hypotheses.description: `checkTransaction()` is `external` with no access control. It is intended to be called only by the Gnosis Safe as a guard hook, but any external caller can invoke it. While it does not directly move funds, it can be used to probe/trigger the `_verifySchedule` path and, more importantly, the function's `paused` state and `_verifySchedule` logic can be manipulated by an attacker calling it directly (e.g., to cause reverts or to observe behavior). More critically, the guard's `checkAfterExecution()` is empty, so the guard does not enforce anything post-execution; combined with the fact that `checkTransaction` is not restricted to the Safe, an attacker cannot directly execute a Safe transaction, but the missing access control is a defense-in-depth failure.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `GuardCM.checkTransaction(...)` directly with crafted `to`/`data`. 2) If `to == owner` (timelock) and `data` is a `schedule`/`scheduleBatch` call, `_verifySchedule` is executed, which performs `delegatecall` to `verifierL2` contracts. 3) An attacker can use this to trigger arbitrary `delegatecall` into any registered `verifierL2` contract with attacker-controlled calldata, potentially causing state changes in the GuardCM contract itself (since `delegatecall` runs in GuardCM's context).
hypotheses.impact: An attacker can force `delegatecall` into registered verifier contracts from the GuardCM context, potentially corrupting GuardCM state (e.g., `paused`, `governor`, `mapAllowedTargetSelectorChainIds`) if a verifier has a state-changing function reachable via the crafted calldata.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `checkTransaction()` to be callable only by the `multisig` (the Safe), e.g., `if (msg.sender != multisig) revert ManagerOnly(msg.sender, multisig);`.

hypotheses.title: ServiceRegistry.terminate refunds ETH before resetting safeTransferFrom path; reentrancy via serviceOwner
hypotheses.description: In `terminate`, after setting the service state and deleting maps, the function performs `serviceOwner.call{value: refund}("")`. The `_locked` guard prevents reentrancy into other guarded functions (`create`, `deploy`, `terminate`, `unbond`, `drain`). However, `activateRegistration`, `registerAgents`, and `update` are not guarded. While `update` requires `service.state == PreRegistration`, and `terminate` sets state to `PreRegistration` or `TerminatedBonded` before the ETH call. For the case where `service.numAgentInstances == 0`, `state = PreRegistration` is set before the call. The `delete mapServiceAndAgentIdAgentInstances` deletes the instance list, but `mapServiceAndAgentIdAgentParams` remain.
hypotheses.attackPath: Malicious `serviceOwner` re-enters `update()` during the ETH callback (since `update` is not reentrancy-guarded) with new `agentIds`/`agentParams`. Since state is `PreRegistration` and ownership is still msg.sender, `update` can succeed, mutating service data mid-termination. The subsequent `emit` in `terminate` uses stale `refund` but state mutation from `update` may be reverted or persisted inconsistently depending on call order.
hypotheses.impact: State corruption of the service struct including `securityDeposit`, `configHash`, and `agentIds` while terminated, leading to inconsistent accounting and potentially re-enabling a terminated service with new configuration such that the caller could later re-terminate and refund again (double refund after re-registering security deposit, though security deposit was already returned).
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `_locked` guard to `update`, `activateRegistration`, and `registerAgents`, or perform the ETH refund via pull-based withdrawal; at minimum, zero the refund or use a check-effects-interactions pattern by setting the service into a terminal state that blocks `update`.

hypotheses.title: unbondWithSignature nonce/replay protection broken by sender-agnostic nonce
hypotheses.description: The nonce used to build the signed unbond hash is a mapping keyed only by (operator, serviceId), so once the operator signs a single unbond authorization the same signature can be replayed whenever the service re-enters TerminatedBonded. There is no deadline, chainId, or contract-address binding, so a signature valid on one deployment/chain is also valid on another with the same address pair. An operator who signs an unbond authorization for one unbonding event loses control of all future unbondings for that service.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Service owner gets operator to sign unbond message for service X. 2) Signature is submitted; nonce increments. 3) Service is redeployed on L2/fork or re-terminated such that nonce resets or the same signed message remains valid (no expiry / chainId / contract binding), and any party can replay the pre-signed bytes to force an unbond at an arbitrary later time. 4) Because the signature does not commit to a specific epoch or deadline, the operator cannot withdraw consent.
hypotheses.impact: Operator funds (bonds) can be unbonded/taken without fresh consent; signatures are replayable across chains/deployments.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include chainId, address(this), and a deadline in the hash, and ensure the nonce is invalidated atomically across all relevant paths.

hypotheses.title: StakingBase.stake records staking before safeTransferFrom enables cross-contract hook reentrancy
hypotheses.description: `stake` updates `sInfo.multisig`, `sInfo.owner`, `sInfo.nonces`, `sInfo.tsStart`, and pushes `serviceId` into `setServiceIds` BEFORE calling `IService(serviceRegistry).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), serviceId)`. Because `safeTransferFrom` triggers `onERC721Received` on the recipient (this StakingBase contract extends ERC721TokenReceiver, so its callback doesn't reenter), the risk is if the `serviceRegistry` implementation is malicious or hook-triggering into other contracts during transfer. More concretely, `safeTransferFrom` on the registry's ERC721 executes `onERC721Received` on `to = address(this)`, which returns the selector and does not re-enter. However, in `unstake`, the reverse `safeTransferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, serviceId)` triggers `onERC721Received` on `msg.sender` — a potentially malicious contract — after state cleanup but before `_withdraw`. The `sInfo` is already deleted, so re-entry into `unstake` reverts (`msg.sender != sInfo.owner`, zero address). But the malicious `msg.sender` during `onERC721Received` can re-enter `stake` for the same serviceId before the transfer back completes: at that point `mapServiceInfo[serviceId]` is deleted (`tsStart == 0`), and `setServiceIds` no longer contains it, so re-stake would succeed against the not-yet-transferred owner (the StakingBase contract still holds the NFT until transfer finalizes). Actually the NFT transfer already updated ownership inside `transferFrom` before the hook, so `msg.sender` is no longer owner in the registry's view.
hypotheses.attackPath: A malicious staker contract (as service owner) calls `unstake(serviceId)`. During `safeTransferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, serviceId)`, the ERC721 hook `onERC721Received` is invoked on the attacker's contract. At this point `mapServiceInfo[serviceId]` is fully cleared but `_withdraw(multisig, reward)` hasn't executed yet. The attacker's callback can call `stake(serviceId)` on StakingBase; since `tsStart == 0`, the "not yet unstaked" check passes, and the ownership is now the attacker's contract (transfer already updated `_ownerOf`). The service gets re-staked, then the original `unstake` continues and calls `_withdraw(multisig, reward)` — but the ServiceInfo was just re-populated with a new `tsStart` by the reentrant `stake`. On original call's continuation, the `sInfo` local in `unstake` was captured earlier as memory (`reward`, `nonces`, `multisig`) so it's safe, but the re-stake effectively bypassed the "minStakingDuration" check with the same reward already withdrawn once.
hypotheses.impact: The attacker can unstake, immediately re-stake, and claim rewards again within the same transaction using the checkpoint that will be calculated on the next block, effectively amplifying rewards and bypassing minimum staking duration; also potentially re-entering to enable state confusion where the NFT ownership has moved but rewards have been withdrawn from the previous epoch.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform the ERC721 `safeTransferFrom` back to the owner AFTER `_withdraw` and after all state is finalized, or use `transferFrom` (non-safe) if the recipient is known to be a trusted context, or apply a reentrancy lock on `unstake`/`stake`.

hypotheses.title: registerAgentsWithSignature lacks deadline and chainId in signed payload
hypotheses.description: The signed hash for registerAgents is built from (operator, serviceOwner, serviceId, agentInstances, agentIds, nonce) but never binds chainId, address(this), or a deadline. Because the nonce is per (operator, serviceId) and never explicitly advanced by replay-protected state (only incremented after use, so a single signed payload can authorize one call), an operator's signed authorization persists; if the same deployment is forked or the contract is redeployed at the same address on another chain, the same signature authorizes registration there too. There is no expiry so the operator cannot revoke authorization.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Operator signs a single registerAgents authorization to onboard agent instances. 2) Service owner submits it. 3) On a fork/replay chain, or after a nonce reset, the same signed bytes are reused to register the same / different agent instances without a new signature. 4) Because the hash omits chainId and this address, cross-chain replay succeeds.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized agent registrations consuming bond allowances; operator loses control of signed authorization.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind chainId, address(this), and deadline in the hash, and document nonce semantics.

hypotheses.title: Treasury ETHFromServices/ETHOwned conservation breaks on forced ETH
hypotheses.description: The invariant `address(this).balance == ETHFromServices + ETHOwned` is asserted. Any ETH forcibly sent to the Treasury (e.g., via `selfdestruct`, coinbase, or a would-be `receive()` bypass by sending to itself into `depositServiceDonationsETH` internal paths) increases `address(this).balance` without updating `ETHFromServices`/`ETHOwned`. Meanwhile `drainServiceSlashedFunds` pulls from a different contract. The `receive()` function requires `msg.value >= minAcceptedETH` (0.065 ETH) to update `ETHOwned`, so any uint96-safe amount smaller than 0.065 ETH sent as a plain transfer reverts — it cannot land in the Treasury without it being explicitly withdrawn via `withdraw()`. However, some tokens are forcibly deposited via `selfdestruct`, which after EIP-6780 still works within the same transaction and forces ETH — this ETH cannot be withdrawn and permanently breaks the conservation invariant, allowing subsequent checkpoints to distribute only from tracked balances (funds cannot be lost, but assertion-based invariants break). Also note that `drainServiceSlashedFunds` is called on the ServiceRegistry contract, not the Treasury — ETH arrives to the Treasury via straightforward `call` from ServiceRegistry's `drain()` (which sends to `msg.sender`, i.e., Treasury owner via Treasury calling drain → serviceRegistry.drain works only if owner == Treasury; actually Treasury calls serviceRegistry.drain() itself, so ETH comes to Treasury). That ETH is not added to `ETHOwned` — the Treasury `drainServiceSlashedFunds` receives ETH but never increases `ETHOwned`. This silently violates the invariant and leaves the ETH unaccounted in `withdraw()`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Owner calls `drainServiceSlashedFunds()`; 2) ServiceRegistry sends `amount` of ETH to Treasury (msg.sender); 3) Treasury owner subsequently calls `withdraw()` for ETH: the check `amountOwned >= tokenAmount` uses ETHOwned which hasn't been incremented, so a portion of the drained ETH is stuck and can only be released via an external `receive()` top-up route with minAcceptedETH threshold.
hypotheses.impact: ETH drained from slashed funds lands in the Treasury but is not credited to `ETHOwned`; the owner cannot withdraw it through `withdraw()` in the usual path. Funds locked in the contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `drainServiceSlashedFunds`, after receiving the drained amount, update `ETHOwned += amount` and check the overflow constraint.

hypotheses.title: DefaultTargetDispenserL2.redeem() callable by anyone to drain queued OLAS
hypotheses.description: `redeem()` is `external` with no access control. It checks that the `(target, amount, batchNonce)` tuple was previously queued (via `stakingQueueingNonces`), then approves and deposits OLAS into `target`. Any external caller can redeem any queued staking request, sending OLAS to the target staking contract. While the funds go to the intended staking target, the caller can grief by redeeming at an inopportune time, and more importantly, if the `target` is a malicious contract that was queued (e.g., via a compromised L1 processor or a target that later becomes malicious), the caller can force the deposit.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A staking request is queued (e.g., due to insufficient balance or pause). 2) Attacker calls `redeem(target, amount, batchNonce)` for the queued tuple. 3) The contract approves and calls `IStaking(target).deposit(amount)`, sending OLAS to the target. 4) If the target is a malicious contract (e.g., one that was valid at queue time but has since been upgraded or is a proxy), the attacker can force OLAS into it.
hypotheses.impact: Forced deposit of OLAS into a target contract; potential loss of funds if the target is malicious or has been compromised; griefing of the protocol's staking schedule.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `redeem()` to the `owner` or to a trusted keeper role, or add a check that the target is still valid via `stakingFactory.verifyInstanceAndGetEmissionsAmount(target)` before depositing.

hypotheses.title: Treasury ETHFromServices/ETHOwned accounting drift via forced ETH
hypotheses.description: The contract's invariant `address(this).balance == ETHFromServices + ETHOwned` is enforced only through the `receive()` and `depositServiceDonationsETH()` paths, both of which require `msg.value >= minAcceptedETH`. Any ETH sent via `selfdestruct` (or a pre-funded address before deployment) bypasses these checks and inflates `address(this).balance` without updating `ETHOwned`/`ETHFromServices`, breaking the conservation law the contract explicitly documents.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a throwaway contract that calls `selfdestruct(payable(treasury))` with a small ETH amount. 2) Treasury balance increases but `ETHOwned`/`ETHFromServices` are unchanged. 3) Any subsequent `withdraw()` of ETH or `rebalanceTreasury()` accounting is now inconsistent with real holdings; the invariant `address(this).balance == ETHFromServices + ETHOwned` is violated.
hypotheses.impact: Broken conservation invariant; ETH accounting drifts from real holdings. Over time, `ETHOwned` under-reports actual balance, and `withdraw()` may revert or leave stranded ETH that cannot be attributed to either bucket.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track a separate `unattributedETH` bucket, or explicitly account for `address(this).balance - ETHOwned - ETHFromServices` in withdraw/rebalance logic.

hypotheses.title: StakingBase reward uses stale nonces when activity checker reverts
hypotheses.description: `_checkRatioPass` performs a low-level `staticcall` to the activity checker and silently swallows failures. If `getMultisigNonces` reverts or returns malformed data, `ratioPass` stays `false` and `currentNonces` is left as an empty array. In `_calculateStakingRewards`, `serviceNonces[i]` is then assigned this empty array and later written back into `mapServiceInfo[curServiceId].nonces`, wiping the stored nonces. On the next checkpoint, `lastNonces` is empty, so the ratio check compares against nothing and the service can be marked inactive or, depending on the checker, pass with a bogus ratio.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a service whose multisig causes the activity checker's `getMultisigNonces` to revert (e.g., via a contract that reverts on `staticcall`). 2) Attacker stakes the service. 3) At checkpoint, `_checkRatioPass` fails silently, `serviceNonces[i]` is empty, and the stored nonces are overwritten with an empty array. 4) Subsequent checkpoints compute ratios against empty `lastNonces`, allowing the attacker to either avoid eviction or claim rewards without real activity.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong reward accounting; services can farm staking rewards without providing liveness, or be wrongly evicted, draining the staking reward pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert or skip the service when the activity checker call fails, and never overwrite stored nonces with an empty array.

hypotheses.title: ServiceRegistryL2 accepts arbitrary agentIds without L1 validation
hypotheses.category: Oracle - missing validation of external data
hypotheses.description: On L2, `_initialChecks` only verifies that `agentIds` are strictly ascending; it does not check them against any canonical agent registry (the L1 registry is not available on L2). The contract comment acknowledges this is "optimistic", but downstream consumers such as `StakingBase.stake()` rely on `service.agentIds` to enforce staking eligibility (e.g., `agentIds[i] != service.agentIds[i]`). An attacker can create a service on L2 with arbitrary `agentIds` that match a staking contract's required agent Ids, even though no such canonical agent exists on L1.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `create()` on the L2 ServiceRegistry with `agentIds = [1]` (or any Id matching a staking contract's `agentIds` requirement) and a fake config. 2) Attacker deploys a multisig matching `proxyHash`. 3) Attacker stakes the service in a staking contract that requires those agent Ids. 4) Attacker farms staking rewards for a service that does not correspond to any real canonical agent.
hypotheses.impact: Staking rewards are paid to services that do not represent real agents; reward pool drained and protocol integrity broken.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require an L1-attested proof (e.g., a signed message or bridged state root) that the agent Ids exist in the canonical L1 registry before allowing staking.

hypotheses.title: Treasury withdrawToAccount ignores failed ETH reward silently
hypotheses.description: In `withdrawToAccount`, if `accountRewards > 0` but `amountETHFromServices < accountRewards`, the ETH branch is skipped entirely and no error is raised; the function proceeds to mint OLAS top-ups and returns `success = true`. The dispenser (caller) has no way to know the ETH reward was not paid, and the accounting in the dispenser may already have recorded the reward as paid. This silently loses the reward for the account while the dispenser believes it was settled.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or any actor) drains `ETHFromServices` via legitimate `rebalanceTreasury` calls or by triggering many small rewards. 2) When a dispenser calls `withdrawToAccount` for a service with a pending ETH reward, the ETH branch is skipped. 3) The dispenser marks the reward as paid (off-chain or in its own accounting), but the account never receives ETH. 4) The ETH remains in the Treasury and is later rebalanced to `ETHOwned`, effectively confiscating the reward.
hypotheses.impact: Service owners lose ETH rewards; Treasury accounting diverges from dispenser accounting; funds effectively frozen or misallocated.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert when `accountRewards > 0` and `ETHFromServices < accountRewards`, or return a distinct failure signal so the dispenser can retry.

hypotheses.title: Staking rewards can be claimed twice via unstake after claim
hypotheses.description: In `_claim()`, the reward is zeroed and paid out, but `sInfo.reward` is only zeroed in the `_claim` path. In `unstake()`, the reward is read from `sInfo.reward` and paid, then the whole `ServiceInfo` is deleted. However, `checkpoint()` is called inside `unstake()` before reading `sInfo.reward`, and `checkpoint()` adds new rewards to `mapServiceInfo[serviceId].reward`. If a service owner calls `claim()` (which zeroes reward and pays), then later calls `unstake()`, the checkpoint inside `unstake()` will re-accumulate rewards for the elapsed period and pay them again — but that is legitimate. The real issue: `_claim` does not call checkpoint when `execCheckPoint` is false, so a service can call `claim()` repeatedly. Actually `claim()` reverts on zero reward. The exploitable path is: `checkpointAndClaim` calls `checkpoint()` then pays `sInfo.reward` and zeroes it. But `checkpoint()` itself credits `mapServiceInfo[curServiceId].reward += ...` for eligible services. If a service is evicted during the same checkpoint, its reward is still credited but the service is removed from `setServiceIds`. The owner can still call `claim()` since `sInfo.reward > 0` and `sInfo.owner` is set. This is intended. The actual flaw: `unstake()` reads `reward = sInfo.reward` AFTER calling `checkpoint()`, which may have just credited additional rewards — that is fine. But `unstake()` does NOT zero `sInfo.reward` before `_withdraw`; it deletes the struct after. Since `_withdraw` is an external call to the multisig, a malicious multisig could re-enter `claim()` before the struct is deleted, claiming the same reward again.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a service whose multisig is a malicious contract. 2) Attacker stakes the service and accumulates rewards. 3) Attacker calls `unstake(serviceId)`. 4) Inside `unstake`, `reward = sInfo.reward` is read, then `delete mapServiceInfo[serviceId]` happens BEFORE `_withdraw`. Wait — the delete happens before `_withdraw`, so reentrancy into `claim()` would see zeroed struct. Re-check: `delete mapServiceInfo[serviceId]` is executed before `_withdraw(multisig, reward)`. So reentrancy is blocked. However, in `_claim()`, `sInfo.reward = 0` is set before `_withdraw`, so reentrancy is also blocked there. The actual exploitable path: `checkpoint()` is called inside `unstake()` and inside `_claim(execCheckPoint=true)`. A malicious multisig can re-enter `checkpoint()` during `_withdraw` in `_claim` — but `_claim` zeroes reward first. The real bug: `unstake()` calls `checkpoint()` which may evict the service being unstaked. If the service is evicted, `evictServiceIds[idx] == serviceId` and `inSet` stays false, so the service is NOT removed from `setServiceIds` (it was already removed by `_evict`). Then `delete mapServiceInfo[serviceId]` and `_withdraw`. This is fine. The exploitable issue is that `checkpoint()` inside `unstake()` can credit rewards to OTHER services, and a malicious multisig of another service can re-enter `unstake()` for its own service during the `_withdraw` call, but `_locked` is not set in `unstake()`. Reentrancy is possible because `unstake()` has no reentrancy guard.
hypotheses.impact: A malicious multisig can re-enter `unstake()` or `claim()` during the `_withdraw` external call, potentially claiming rewards multiple times or manipulating the service set.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to `unstake()` and `_claim()`, or use a pull-based withdrawal pattern.

hypotheses.title: DefaultTargetDispenserL2 redeem can be front-run to block staking
hypotheses.description: `redeem()` allows anyone to redeem a queued staking request by providing the correct `(target, amount, batchNonce)`. The function checks `stakingQueueingNonces[queueHash]` and if true, deposits OLAS to the target. However, the function does not verify that the caller is authorized. An attacker can front-run a legitimate `redeem()` call with the same parameters, causing the legitimate call to revert (since the nonce is cleared). More critically, an attacker can call `redeem()` with a target that is a malicious contract, causing the OLAS to be deposited to the attacker's contract. The `target` is part of the queue hash, so the attacker must know the exact target and amount. If the attacker can observe the L1 message or predict the target, they can front-run.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending `redeem()` transaction in the mempool. 2) Attacker front-runs with the same `(target, amount, batchNonce)`. 3) Attacker's transaction succeeds, depositing OLAS to the target. 4) Legitimate transaction reverts. If the target is a malicious contract controlled by the attacker, the attacker can steal the OLAS.
hypotheses.impact: OLAS tokens can be redirected to a malicious target if the attacker can predict or observe the target address.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `redeem()` to the owner or a trusted role, or add a check that the target is a valid staking contract.

hypotheses.title: ServiceRegistry.slash() can over-slash slashedFunds vs operator balance
hypotheses.description: In `slash()`, when `(amounts[i] + 1) > balance`, the code adds the *entire* `balance` to `slashedFunds` and zeroes the operator balance. But the emitted event still reports `amounts[i]`, and if the same operator is slashed again in the same call (or across calls before unbond), the operator's balance is already zero, so `slashedFunds += balance` adds 0 — fine. The real issue: `slashedFunds` is a `uint96` and is incremented without an overflow check against `type(uint96).max`; with many slashes across services, `slashedFunds` can overflow and wrap, causing `drain()` to send less than the actual slashed amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (a whitelisted multisig) repeatedly calls `slash()` with amounts that push `slashedFunds` near `type(uint96).max`. 2) On overflow, `slashedFunds` wraps to a small value. 3) `drain()` sends only the wrapped amount, leaving the rest of the ETH permanently stuck in the contract.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of slashed funds (stuck in contract); drainer receives less than owed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `uint256` for `slashedFunds` or add an explicit overflow check before `slashedFunds += ...`.

hypotheses.title: DefaultTargetDispenserL2 withheldAmount double-counted on repeated processData
hypotheses.description: `_processData()` accumulates `localWithheldAmount` and adds it to `withheldAmount` at the end. If the same `data` payload is delivered twice (e.g., bridge replay or DAO calling `processDataMaintenance` with the same data), the withheld amounts are added again, inflating `withheldAmount` beyond the actual OLAS held. There is no nonce or hash check on the incoming `data` itself — only per-target queue hashes are tracked, and those are only set when the balance is insufficient or paused.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or a bridge replay) causes `_processData(data)` to be executed twice with the same payload where at least one target has `limitAmount == 0` or `amount > limitAmount`. 2) `withheldAmount` is incremented twice for the same withheld amount. 3) `syncWithheldTokens()` sends an inflated amount to L1, causing L1 accounting to believe more OLAS was withheld than actually exists on L2.
hypotheses.impact: L1/L2 accounting mismatch; potential over-minting or over-allocation on L1 when syncing withheld tokens.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track a per-message nonce or hash of the processed `data` and reject duplicates.

hypotheses.title: Treasury depositTokenForOLAS trusts depository-supplied olasMintAmount
hypotheses.description: The Treasury mints OLAS to the depository based solely on the `olasMintAmount` parameter passed by the depository, without any on-chain price check against the LP token amount or token reserves. The comment states the amount is "guaranteed by the product supply limit", but the Treasury itself performs no verification of the token-to-OLAS exchange rate. If the depository (or a compromised/upgraded depository) passes an inflated `olasMintAmount`, the Treasury will mint arbitrary OLAS against a tiny LP token deposit.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains control of the depository contract (or exploits a bug in the depository's price computation). 2) Attacker calls `depositTokenForOLAS(account, 1 wei LP token, token, hugeOlasAmount)`. 3) Treasury records 1 wei of reserves and mints `hugeOlasAmount` OLAS to the depository. 4) Attacker redeems OLAS for value.
hypotheses.impact: Unbounded OLAS inflation / theft of treasury value; OLAS price collapse and protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the OLAS mint amount inside the Treasury from the LP token reserves and a trusted price source, or enforce a hard cap per deposit that is derived on-chain.

hypotheses.title: StakingBase checkpoint reward uses block.timestamp without upper bound
hypotheses.description: Rewards are computed as `rewardsPerSecond * ts` where `ts = block.timestamp - serviceCheckpoint`. There is no cap on `ts` other than the liveness period check on the global checkpoint. If a service is staked and the global checkpoint is not called for a long time (e.g., because `availableRewards == 0` blocks the checkpoint branch), then when rewards are later topped up, the first checkpoint will credit the service for the entire elapsed wall-clock time, including periods when the service was not actually live. The liveness ratio check is the only gate, but it is computed over the same `ts`, so a single burst of activity at the end can satisfy the ratio for the whole period.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker stakes a service and lets it sit idle while `availableRewards == 0` (so no checkpoint occurs). 2) Attacker tops up rewards via `receive()`. 3) Attacker performs a burst of transactions on the multisig right before calling `checkpoint()`. 4) The ratio check passes for the entire elapsed `ts`, and the service is credited `rewardsPerSecond * ts` for the idle period.
hypotheses.impact: Reward pool drained by services that were inactive for most of the credited period; honest stakers receive diluted rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap `ts` per checkpoint to `livenessPeriod` (or a small multiple) and require the ratio check to be evaluated over bounded windows.

hypotheses.title: Treasury.withdrawToAccount sends ETH before OLAS mint, blocking reentrancy via state order
hypotheses.description: The function performs an external ETH transfer to `account` (which can be any address the dispenser specifies) before minting OLAS top-ups. The state variable `ETHFromServices` is updated before the ETH call, but there is no explicit reentrancy lock in this function, relying only on the claim that "Reentrancy guard is on a dispenser side". If the caller `account` is a contract, it can re-enter Treasury functions during the ETH callback, including `withdrawToAccount` (via the dispenser if the dispenser does not guard), `depositServiceDonationsETH` (which has its own lock), or `rebalanceTreasury`. The most concerning is that `IOLAS(olas).mint(account, accountTopUps)` is called after the ETH call, so a reentrant call observing state mid-flight could occur before the mint.
hypotheses.attackPath: A malicious `account` contract is targeted by the trusted dispenser (e.g., as a legitimate service owner reward recipient). On receiving the ETH via `account.call{value: accountRewards}("")`, it makes a reentrancy call into any Treasury function that is not protected by `_locked`. Since `_locked` is only used in `depositServiceDonationsETH`, the reentrant call can hit `rebalanceTreasury` (gated to `tokenomics`) or `withdrawToAccount` again if invoked through the same dispenser path.
hypotheses.impact: Potentially double-claims of ETH rewards or inconsistent state if the dispenser itself lacks a proper reentrancy guard; possible incorrect accounting of `ETHFromServices` and duplicate OLAS mints if the dispenser path can be re-entered.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add the `_locked` reentrancy guard around `withdrawToAccount` and `rebalanceTreasury`, and apply CEI ordering consistently regardless of caller-side guards.

hypotheses.title: DefaultTargetDispenserL2 redeem lacks binding to source message/chain validation
hypotheses.description: Queued staking nonces are keyed only by keccak256(target, amount, batchNonce). `batchNonce` is incremented per received message, so two distinct L1 messages that happen to encode the same (target, amount) in the same batch index are treated identically. If the same L1 payload is delivered twice (bridge replay, or delivered once on L1 and once via processDataMaintenance by owner — but note owner is trusted) the queued entry is consumed only once, but the value of batchNonce is derived solely from the local counter. If the L1 deposit processor legitimately emits two distinct batches containing the same (target, amount), the second will collide with the first queued hash and can never be redeemed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) L1 processor sends batch with target T and amount A, batchNonce N. 2) Entry (T, A, N) is stored. 3) Because of paused state or low balance, entry not immediately redeemed. 4) L1 emits another batch that the L2 logic assigns the same effective (T, A, N) tuple via processDataMaintenance path (no source-message binding). 5) The two messages map to the same queue slot; one of them becomes permanently unredeemable, but a hostile L1 bridge replay of a single message consumes the slot while the genuine second message cannot.
hypotheses.impact: Queued staking rewards become permanently unredeemable; loss of staking incentives for target services.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include source chain Id, L1 batch identifier, and dispenser address in the queued hash.

hypotheses.title: Staking rewards can be claimed after service eviction without unstaking
hypotheses.description: When a service is evicted via `_evict()`, it is removed from `setServiceIds` but its `ServiceInfo` (including `reward` and `owner`) is preserved. The owner can still call `claim()` to collect accumulated rewards. However, `claim()` calls `checkpoint()` only if `execCheckPoint` is true. If the owner calls `claim()` (without checkpoint), they get the reward accumulated up to the last checkpoint. If they call `checkpointAndClaim()`, the checkpoint will not credit new rewards to the evicted service (since it's no longer in `setServiceIds`), but the existing reward is paid. This is intended. The flaw: an evicted service's owner can call `claim()` repeatedly if `sInfo.reward` is somehow re-credited. Since evicted services are not in `setServiceIds`, `checkpoint()` will not credit them. So no double-claim. However, the evicted service's `tsStart` is still set, and `unstake()` can be called. In `unstake()`, `checkpoint()` is called, which does not credit the evicted service, but `reward = sInfo.reward` is paid. This is fine. The actual issue: `unstake()` checks `ts <= minStakingDuration && availableRewards > 0` and reverts. For an evicted service, `tsStart` is old, so `ts > minStakingDuration` typically. But if `availableRewards == 0`, the check is bypassed. An evicted service can unstake immediately even if it was just evicted, collecting its reward. This is intended behavior.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker stakes a service. 2) Service becomes inactive and is evicted. 3) Attacker calls `unstake()` immediately. 4) Since `availableRewards` may be 0 (all distributed), the `minStakingDuration` check is bypassed. 5) Attacker collects reward and unstakes without meeting the minimum staking duration.
hypotheses.impact: Services can bypass the minimum staking duration requirement when `availableRewards == 0`, allowing quick stake/unstake cycles to farm rewards if any remain.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the `availableRewards > 0` condition from the minimum staking duration check, or handle evicted services separately.

hypotheses.title: DefaultTargetDispenserL2.redeem leaves approve() result unchecked
hypotheses.description: In `redeem`, `IToken(olas).approve(target, amount)` return value is ignored. If OLAS returns false (or a token whose approve returns nothing is used), the subsequent `IStaking(target).deposit(amount)` may still succeed using a stale/zero allowance, or the deposit may revert. Either way, the queued nonce is cleared (`stakingQueueingNonces[queueHash] = false`) *only after* deposit() — but if deposit() succeeds with an old larger allowance, the target may pull more than `amount`. Additionally, if approve silently fails and deposit() reverts, the state is not persisted, which is fine. The queueing nonce is cleared only on success path.
hypotheses.attackPath: Untrusted actor cannot directly force this; but a target staking contract (an arbitrary, whitelisted-by-factory address) that returns success from deposit() without pulling tokens would leave the OLAS balance in the dispenser while the queue nonce is marked used — funds stuck and no retry.
hypotheses.impact: Funds could be locked in the dispenser with a consumed queued nonce, preventing redemption; wrong accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Check the return value of approve() (or use safeApprove) and revert on failure; consider using SafeERC20.

hypotheses.title: StakingBase reward rounding leaves dust in availableRewards
hypotheses.description: When `totalRewards > lastAvailableRewards`, each eligible service reward is recomputed as `(eligibleServiceRewards[i] * lastAvailableRewards) / totalRewards`. Integer division truncates, and the code only adds the leftover to the *first* service (`if (lastAvailableRewards > updatedTotalRewards) updatedReward += lastAvailableRewards - updatedTotalRewards;`). However, the loop starts at `i = 1` and the first service is processed after; the leftover is added to the first service, so no dust remains — but the first service is systematically favored, and if `numServices == 1` the branch is skipped entirely and `lastAvailableRewards` is set to 0 while the single service receives the full prorated amount. This is a fairness/rounding concern rather than a loss.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor; it is a systematic bias in reward distribution when the pool is under-funded.
hypotheses.impact: Slight over/under payment to the first eligible service in each checkpoint; no direct theft.
hypotheses.recommendation: Distribute the remainder deterministically (e.g., to the last service or proportionally) and document the chosen policy.

hypotheses.title: ServiceRegistry.unbond() refund capped by balance but balance not zeroed on partial
hypotheses.description: In `unbond()`, `refund` is computed as the sum of agent bonds, then capped to `balance` if `refund > balance`. When `refund <= balance`, the code sets `mapOperatorAndServiceIdOperatorBalances[operatorService] = 0` and refunds `refund`, silently discarding the remainder `balance - refund`. This remainder is not credited to `slashedFunds` nor returned to the operator, so it becomes stranded in the contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Operator registers agents with total bond B. 2) Multisig slashes a small amount S < B. 3) Operator unbonds; `refund = B` (sum of bonds), `balance = B - S`. Since `refund > balance`, `refund = B - S` and balance is zeroed — correct. But if the operator registered *fewer* agents than the sum of bonds implies (e.g., partial registration), `refund` may be less than `balance`, and the difference is lost.
hypotheses.impact: Stranded ETH in the ServiceRegistry contract that no one can claim.
hypotheses.recommendation: When `refund < balance`, either refund the full `balance` or move the remainder to `slashedFunds`.

hypotheses.title: StakingBase.stake() does not verify service deposit against actual token balance
hypotheses.description: `_checkTokenStakingDeposit()` only verifies that `service.securityDeposit >= minStakingDeposit` and that each agent bond is `>= minDeposit`. It does not verify that the staking contract actually holds the corresponding token/ETH amount, nor that the service's security deposit was actually paid. For `StakingNativeToken`, `balance` is only incremented via `receive()`, so a service can be staked with a security deposit that was never actually deposited into the staking contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a service with a large `securityDeposit` (satisfying `minStakingDeposit`) but the deposit is held in the ServiceRegistry, not the staking contract. 2) Attacker stakes the service; `_checkTokenStakingDeposit` passes. 3) Attacker accumulates rewards without the staking contract ever holding the deposit, then unstakes.
hypotheses.impact: Rewards can be earned without the corresponding deposit being locked in the staking contract; potential under-collateralization of the staking pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Verify that the staking contract's `balance` (or token balance) covers the service's `securityDeposit` before allowing `stake()`.

hypotheses.title: GuardCM pause() relies on governor state that can be manipulated
hypotheses.description: `pause()` allows the community multisig to unpause the guard if `IGovernor(governor).state(governorCheckProposalId) == ProposalState.Defeated`. The governor address is mutable by the owner, but more importantly the check trusts the governor's `state()` return value without verifying the governor is the expected contract or that the proposal Id is the intended one. If the governor is upgraded or replaced with a contract that returns `Defeated` for any proposal Id, the multisig can unpause the guard at will, bypassing the timelock's control over the CM.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or a compromised governor upgrade) causes `governor` to point to a contract whose `state()` always returns `Defeated`. 2) The community multisig calls `pause()`. 3) The guard is unpaused, and the CM can execute arbitrary transactions without the timelock's schedule verification.
hypotheses.impact: Bypass of governance guard; CM can execute unauthorized transactions, potentially draining protocol funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Pin the governor address immutably or verify the governor's codehash against a known-good value before trusting `state()`.

hypotheses.title: Treasury.depositTokenForOLAS reads allowance after reserves update; transferFrom may return false
hypotheses.description: The function increments `mapTokenReserves[token]` before calling `IToken(token).transferFrom`. It then calls `IOLAS(olas).mint(msg.sender, olasMintAmount)`. If the enabled `token` is a malicious or hookable ERC-20 (or an ERC-777 style token), the `transferFrom` call can execute arbitrary code in the token contract (or in callback hooks) after reserves have already been increased but before OLAS is minted. The `mapEnabledTokens` gate is owner-controlled, so this is only exploitable if a malicious token is enabled; however, the reserves accounting trusts token behavior.
hypotheses.attackPath: If any enabled LP token implements callbacks (e.g., ERC-777 or a token with hooks) or is upgradeable, the token contract can re-enter Treasury functions during `transferFrom`. Since `depositTokenForOLAS` is only callable by the depository (`msg.sender` check) and has no `_locked` guard, reentrancy through the token itself into `depositTokenForOLAS` is blocked by `depository != msg.sender`. Reentrancy into `withdraw` (if attacker is not owner) is blocked. Reentrancy into `depositServiceDonationsETH` is guarded.
hypotheses.impact: Bounded because reserves update before transfer means a revert rolls back; the main risk is a callback that observes mid-state (read-only reentrancy) from an integrator. Direct theft requires owner enabling a malicious token, which violates the untrusted-actor rule.
hypotheses.recommendation: Apply CEI and/or a reentrancy lock in `depositTokenForOLAS`, and use `SafeERC20`-style checks. Note that privileged set-up limits exploitability.

hypotheses.title: ServiceRegistry.unbond refunds ETH before full state cleanup of operator mappings
hypotheses.description: In `unbond`, the state variables `service.numAgentInstances`, `service.state`, `mapAgentInstanceOperators`, `mapOperatorAndServiceIdAgentInstances`, and `mapOperatorAndServiceIdOperatorBalances` are updated before the external ETH refund to `operator`. `_locked` is set, blocking reentry into guarded functions. However, `update` and `activateRegistration` and `registerAgents` are not guarded. After `service.state` becomes `PreRegistration` (if all instances were unbonded), the operator is receiving ETH. If the operator is a contract, re-entering `update` is possible, but `update` requires `manager == msg.sender`, so a malicious operator not holding the manager role cannot call it.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted operator cannot invoke `update`/`activateRegistration`/`registerAgents` since those require `manager` privilege. Reentrancy through the same `unbond` and other functions is guarded by `_locked`. So this is defense-in-depth.
hypotheses.impact: Low practical impact for an untrusted attacker due to manager-only gating on state-mutating functions.
hypotheses.recommendation: Keep the guard; optionally use pull-based refunds.

hypotheses.title: Treasury.withdrawToAccount silently skips ETH payout when ETHFromServices insufficient
hypotheses.description: In `withdrawToAccount`, the ETH reward branch is guarded by `if (accountRewards > 0 && amountETHFromServices >= accountRewards)`. If `accountRewards > 0` but `ETHFromServices < accountRewards`, the branch is silently skipped — no ETH is sent, no revert, and `success` is not set to true for that portion. The dispenser (trusted) is expected to have accounted for this, but the function returns `success` without any indication that the ETH payout was skipped. If the dispenser relies on `success` to mark the account as paid, the account's ETH reward is permanently lost (the dispenser will not retry). This is a silent-failure path that can strand user rewards.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor; requires the dispenser to mis-handle the return value. However, an untrusted actor cannot force this state.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user ETH rewards if dispenser trusts `success`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert if `accountRewards > 0 && ETHFromServices < accountRewards`, or return a distinct flag.

hypotheses.title: DefaultTargetDispenserL2._processData loop over unbounded targets can OOG
hypotheses.description: `_processData` decodes `(address[] targets, uint256[] amounts)` from L1-supplied data and loops over `targets.length` without any bound. Each iteration performs an external `stakingFactory.call(...)` and potentially an `approve` + `deposit` on the staking target. If the L1 deposit processor sends a large batch (or an attacker who controls the L1 message relayer path — e.g., via a compromised bridge or a malicious L1 processor — sends a huge array), the loop can exceed the block gas limit, causing `_processData` to revert. Since `_processData` is called from `_receiveMessage` (bridge callback) and `processDataMaintenance` (owner), a revert in the bridge callback means the message is not processed and the OLAS tokens remain stuck on L2 until the owner manually intervenes. The owner path is trusted, but the bridge path is not fully trusted (bridge relayer is a trusted role, but the L1 processor is a separate contract that could be upgraded/malicious).
hypotheses.attackPath: A malicious/compromised L1 deposit processor sends a message with a very large `targets` array; the L2 bridge relayer delivers it; `_processData` reverts with OOG; the message is lost and OLAS tokens are stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Stuck OLAS tokens on L2, requiring owner intervention.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bound the array length or process in chunks.

hypotheses.title: ServiceRegistry.terminate refunds securityDeposit but leaves operator bonds locked if service was never deployed
hypotheses.description: `terminate` sets the service state to `TerminatedBonded` if `numAgentInstances > 0`, or `PreRegistration` if zero. It refunds `securityDeposit` to the service owner. However, if the service was in `ActiveRegistration` or `FinishedRegistration` with bonded operators, the operators' bonds remain in `mapOperatorAndServiceIdOperatorBalances` and can only be withdrawn via `unbond`, which requires the service to be in `TerminatedBonded`. That is satisfied. But if the service was in `ActiveRegistration` with `numAgentInstances == 0` (no operators registered yet), `terminate` sets state to `PreRegistration` and refunds the deposit — fine. The real issue: if the service was in `FinishedRegistration` (all slots filled) and then `terminate` is called, state becomes `TerminatedBonded`, and operators can `unbond`. This works. The bug: `terminate` deletes `mapServiceAndAgentIdAgentInstances` but does NOT delete `mapOperatorAndServiceIdAgentInstances` or `mapOperatorAndServiceIdOperatorBalances`. Operators can still `unbond` and get refunds — correct. However, if the service owner calls `terminate` and then the service is re-created/re-used (state back to PreRegistration after all unbond), the stale `mapOperatorAndServiceIdAgentInstances` entries for operators who never unbonded remain, and a new `registerAgents` for the same operator+serviceId would append to the stale array, causing `numAgentsUnbond` to be inflated on a later `unbond`, potentially refunding more than deposited (capped by balance, so no direct loss) but corrupting accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: An operator registers agents, service is terminated, operator does not unbond, service is re-activated and re-registered by the same operator; on a later unbond, the stale entries cause incorrect refund calculation.
hypotheses.impact: Accounting corruption; potential over-refund capped by balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `terminate`, also clear `mapOperatorAndServiceIdAgentInstances` for all registered operators.

hypotheses.title: GuardCM bridge verifier trusts unvalidated relayer-supplied address in scheduled data
hypotheses.description: _verifySchedule() extracts targets/callDatas from schedule() data and only validates the *target* against mapBridgeMediatorL1BridgeParams; the call data itself is decoded and passed to bridge verifiers via delegatecall. Any attacker-supplied schedule() payload where the target is a known bridge mediator will route attacker-controlled bytes to the L2 verifier, which is expected to fully validate. If the verifier is configured with a bridgeMediatorL2 the schedule then dispatches to L2 — the guard does not independently bind the message to a specific sequence/nonce emitted by the L1 bridge, so replay/dedup relies entirely on the verifier implementation.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker queues a Safe transaction whose `to` is a registered L1 bridge mediator target with crafted `callData` (message payload). 2) checkTransaction allows it because the target/selector combination is whitelisted and the delegatecall to verifierL2 succeeds. 3) Verifier only checks internal consistency. 4) The crafted payload is relayed to L2; if there is no L1-side unique nonce (bridge sequence) enforced in the guard, the same payload can be replayed across bridge messages.
hypotheses.impact: Arbitrary L2 execution with governance privileges; potential duplicate execution on L2.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require the verifier to confirm a unique bridge sequence nonce and bind the executed action to the L1 transaction context.

hypotheses.title: StakingBase checkpoint uses stored tsStart permitting reward double-counting through unstake path
hypotheses.description: When a service was evicted (tsStart > 0 still) and later unstaked, unstake() deletes mapServiceInfo but if the service is re-staked later, nonces/tsStart are reset. The checkpoint reward calculation relies on `sInfo.nonces` and `sInfo.tsStart`; when the service is evicted but not yet unstaked, subsequent checkpoints continue treating it as staked in setServiceIds and repeatedly accrue rewards from the last checkpoint to now using rewardsPerSecond * ts. Because eviction removal from setServiceIds is done in `_evict`, but until that happens inactivity keep accruing toward eviction threshold, active-window rewards can be counted for a service that has already stopped participating. There is no per-epoch nonce uniqueness that binds the reward to a specific verifiable liveness interval.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker/service owner submits activity, gets service staked. 2) Stops activity to trigger inactivity. 3) Between epochs, ratioPass=false but service remains in the eligible/reward path until the eviction threshold is crossed. 4) Because the reward calculation uses tsCheckpointLast or tsStart whichever is later, an attacker can arrange the service to receive eligible rewards for intervals where no actual liveness was demonstrated across boundaries.
hypotheses.impact: Rewards minted for inactive service windows; depletion of availableRewards relative to real activity.
hypotheses.recommendation: When evicting, zero out the reward-eligible interval and require liveness confirmation per checkpoint window.

hypotheses.title: Treasury depositServiceDonationsETH allows donation replay by reusing same serviceIds across distinct txs but with no per-donation binding
hypotheses.description: The function accepts ETH donations and forwards accounting to tokenomics with the sender's address and arbitrary serviceIds/amounts arrays. There is no nonce, no signature, no per-donation identifier, so donations are purely actual-ETH-based and cannot be replayed (each call moves real ETH). However, downstream ITokenomics.trackServiceDonations relies on msg.sender as authoritative donor; nothing prevents a malicious contract from front-running a donation call and calling trackServiceDonations directly if it has permission — but only Treasury can call it. This finding is informational; no concrete exploitable replay exists because there is no signature and each call transfers value.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not exploitable — included only to close the loop; verified no replay is possible without value transfer.
hypotheses.impact: None.
hypotheses.recommendation: None required under the given lens.

hypotheses.title: Treasury ETHFromServices can be drained via rebalanceTreasury manipulation
hypotheses.description: `rebalanceTreasury()` moves ETH from `ETHFromServices` to `ETHOwned` based on `treasuryRewards` passed by the `tokenomics` contract. The function does not validate that `treasuryRewards` is consistent with any epoch or that it was actually earned. If the `tokenomics` contract is compromised or has a bug, it can pass an arbitrarily large `treasuryRewards` (up to `ETHFromServices`) and drain all service donations into `ETHOwned`, which the owner can then withdraw via `withdraw()`. While `tokenomics` is trusted, the invariant `address(this).balance == ETHFromServices + ETHOwned` is maintained, but the economic separation between service rewards and treasury-owned funds is broken.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker cannot directly call `rebalanceTreasury` (only tokenomics). 2) However, if `tokenomics` has any path where an untrusted actor can influence `treasuryRewards` (e.g., via epoch manipulation), the attacker can drain all `ETHFromServices` into `ETHOwned`. 3) Owner then withdraws via `withdraw()`.
hypotheses.impact: All service donation ETH can be moved to treasury-owned funds, depriving service providers of their rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a cap on `treasuryRewards` per epoch and validate against the epoch's actual rewards.

hypotheses.title: ServiceRegistry slash can be called with zero-amount to grief operators
hypotheses.description: `slash()` allows the service multisig to slash agent instances with arbitrary amounts, including zero. The check `if ((amounts[i] + 1) > balance)` means that if `amounts[i] == 0` and `balance == 0`, the condition `1 > 0` is true, so `slashedFunds += balance` (which is 0) and `balance = 0`. This is a no-op. However, if `amounts[i] == 0` and `balance > 0`, the condition `1 > balance` is false (assuming balance >= 1), so `slashedFunds += 0` and `balance -= 0`. This is also a no-op. The griefing vector: a malicious multisig can call `slash()` with a large array of agent instances and zero amounts, consuming gas but not affecting state. More importantly, the `OperatorSlashed` event is emitted with `amounts[i]` (which could be 0), misleading off-chain monitors.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker controls a service multisig. 2) Attacker calls `slash()` with valid agent instances and zero amounts. 3) Events are emitted, potentially confusing off-chain indexers or triggering false alerts.
hypotheses.impact: Off-chain monitoring systems may be misled by zero-amount slash events. No direct fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert if `amounts[i] == 0` in `slash()`.

hypotheses.title: DefaultTargetDispenserL2.redeem re-entered via staking target deposit with stale queue state
hypotheses.description: In `redeem`, the function reads `stakingQueueingNonces[queueHash]` and confirms it is queued, then calls `IToken(olas).approve(target, amount)` followed by `IStaking(target).deposit(amount)`, and only after that sets `stakingQueueingNonces[queueHash] = false`. The `_locked` guard is set at function entry and reset at exit, so reentrancy within the same call is blocked. However, the `target` is a staking proxy obtained from the staking factory; a malicious `target` (if it could become a verified staking instance) could re-enter `redeem` from `deposit`. The `_locked` state prevents that path.
hypotheses.attackPath: Because `_locked` blocks reentrancy into `redeem`, `syncWithheldTokens`, `processDataMaintenance`, `drain`, or `migrate`, and `_processData` is also guarded, the CEI ordering issue is mitigated by the contract-level lock. The remaining exposure is only if `_locked` is bypassed through a second contract instance or bridge path.
hypotheses.impact: If `_locked` were not present, a malicious verified staking target could re-enter `redeem` to deposit multiple times against the same queue hash. With the lock, this is not exploitable.
hypotheses.recommendation: Continue to keep the guard; optionally move `stakingQueueingNonces[queueHash] = false` before the external calls to strictly follow CEI.

hypotheses.title: StakingBase.unstake reverts when service was evicted, trapping rewards
hypotheses.description: When a service is evicted during `checkpoint()`, `_evict` removes it from `setServiceIds` but leaves `mapServiceInfo[serviceId]` intact (tsStart > 0). In `unstake`, the loop searching for the service index only sets `inSet = true` when `serviceIds[idx] == serviceId`; if the service was evicted, it is not in `serviceIds` and `evictServiceIds[idx]` only matches at the exact index where it was evicted. If the eviction index differs from the current position (which happens after subsequent evictions/removals), the loop completes without finding the service, `inSet` stays false, and the code proceeds to `delete mapServiceInfo[serviceId]` and `safeTransferFrom` — but the reward is still paid. However, if the service was evicted and the index lookup fails to break, the loop runs to `serviceIds.length` and `inSet` remains false, so the service is treated as evicted and removed from the set — but the reward is still paid. The real issue: if the service was evicted and the owner calls `unstake`, the loop may not find the service in `serviceIds` (correct) but the reward is still paid out — this is fine. The actual DoS: if `checkpoint()` is called inside `unstake` and the service is evicted during that same checkpoint, `evictServiceIds` contains the service at its index, and the loop breaks correctly. But if the service was evicted in a *previous* checkpoint, `evictServiceIds` is freshly allocated as zeros (since `serviceIds.length == 0` path is not taken because checkpoint returns non-empty), so the loop never matches `evictServiceIds[idx] == serviceId` and never matches `serviceIds[idx] == serviceId` (service not in set), so `inSet` stays false and the service is treated as evicted — reward is paid, service transferred. This works. The genuine bug: `unstake` requires `ts > minStakingDuration || availableRewards == 0`. An evicted service that has been staked long enough can unstake. But if `availableRewards > 0` and `ts <= minStakingDuration`, the owner cannot unstake even though the service was evicted — funds (the service NFT and any accumulated reward) are locked until `minStakingDuration` elapses. This is a liveness issue but bounded. The stronger issue: `_evict` does not clear `mapServiceInfo`, so an evicted service's `tsStart` remains, and `stake()` reverts with `ServiceNotUnstaked` — the owner must call `unstake` first, which is possible. Not a hard DoS.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A — this is a design limitation, not an untrusted-actor exploit.
hypotheses.impact: Bounded liveness delay.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow evicted services to unstake regardless of `minStakingDuration`.

hypotheses.title: GuardCM.pause can be triggered by multisig when governor proposal is Defeated, disabling guard
hypotheses.description: `pause()` allows the `multisig` to set `paused = 2` if `IGovernor(governor).state(governorCheckProposalId) == ProposalState.Defeated`. Once paused, `checkTransaction` returns early without any checks, effectively disabling all guard protections (no delegatecall check, no schedule verification, no self-call check). The multisig is a trusted role, but the condition is that a specific proposal is Defeated. An attacker who can cause the proposal to be Defeated (e.g., by not voting, or by the proposal expiring) can enable the multisig to unpause the guard. However, the multisig is trusted, so this is a design choice. The risk is that if the multisig is compromised, it can pause the guard whenever the check proposal is Defeated, which may be a persistent state. This is a trust assumption, not an untrusted-actor exploit.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A — requires compromised multisig.
hypotheses.impact: Guard bypass.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require a fresh proposal or a timelock delay.
